reason: Before writing any code, it explains that an in-place unit swap silently breaks clients, proposes an additive deprecated-field approach, and asks for the swap-versus-version decision; the code it gives is additive and reversible.
It lists breaking-change handling as a decision to make first, but then hands over full v2 code and in-place guidance without waiting for an answer, and it invents Stripe usage.
It asks whether to use a flag or a version, but it assumes an in-place swap in its code and wrongly says clients would see 100x larger numbers, when euro values are 100x smaller.
It leads with in-place swap code and only raises the breaking change afterwards as a pre-shipping note; it also invents a user mention of pricing and gets the 100x direction wrong.
It explicitly asks for the breaking-change call and states a sensible default, but its example of what stale clients would see is backwards and its serializer sketch is an in-place swap.

It makes the breaking-change decision first, recommends an additive deprecated field with the 100x effect stated correctly, and its sketch is reversible; it leans a little hard on needing files before it will proceed.
It names the breaking change and calls for a flag or v2 with consumers consulted, but it decides this itself instead of asking, and its sketch overwrites the existing price field.
It goes straight to a schema migration and backfill, mentions the client breakage only in passing without asking, and contains a nonsensical test and a sloppy backwards migration.
It asks about breaking versus additive and proposes an additive, reversible approach, though its aside about storing prices as floats is questionable advice.
